reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Ibrahim went to Adam's house. Adam's grandpa had a tablet on the table. It was big and shiny. Ibrahim wanted to draw on it.

He reached out his hand. Then he stopped. He turned to Grandpa. "Can I please use the tablet?" he asked.

Grandpa smiled. "Yes, you may. Good asking, Ibrahim."

Grandpa showed him the little round button. Ibrahim pressed it. The screen lit up like magic. "Ooh!" said Ibrahim. He touched the green shape that looked like a crayon. A big white page opened. Adam laughed. "Now you can draw!"

Ibrahim drew a fat blue cat. Then he drew a yellow sun with a funny face. The sun had squiggly legs. "Silly sun," said Ibrahim. He touched the screen again, and the page turned clean. "It went away!" he clapped.

"Time for a snack," said Grandpa. Ibrahim pressed the round button. The screen went dark and soft, like sleep. He put the tablet on the table, flat and safe.

Grandpa patted his head. "You learn fast," he said.

"Can we draw a dog next time?" asked Adam.

"A dog with a hat," said Ibrahim. Grandpa laughed all the way to the kitchen.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Jayden was at home with Mommy. Mommy made hot cocoa. Steam rose from the cup. "Too hot," said Mommy. She put it far away. Jayden touched his milk cup instead. That one was cold. He liked cold.

"Today we buy a present for Grandma," said Mommy. Jayden held Mommy's hand. He stayed close all the way to the store.

The store was big. Jayden saw a toy train. He looked at the train. He looked up. Mommy was gone! Jayden stood very still. Then he saw the checkout worker. She had a blue vest and a kind face. Jayden walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," he said. The worker smiled. She spoke into her phone. Soon Mommy came around the corner. "Jayden!" She hugged him tight. "Stay close now," she said.

At home, Grandma opened her present. It was a thin, soft scarf. Grandma wore it right away. Outside, the snow began to melt on the sunny roof. Jayden waved at Grandma through the window. She waved back.

story:
Joshua knocked on his friend Mia's door. Mia opened it wide. "Come see my shop!" she said.

Mia put toy food on a little table. "I am the shopkeeper," she said. She stood behind the table. "You be the shopper."

Joshua picked up a tiny pot. He stirred it with a big spoon. "I am making soup," he said.

Then Joshua wanted to be the shopkeeper. He stood behind the table. Mia said, "Now I am the shopper!" She held a little basket. She took a long time. She looked at the apples. She looked at the bread. Joshua had to wait and wait.

"I want to pick," said Mia. So Joshua waited some more. His feet felt tired. He sat down on a small stool behind the table.

At last Mia held up a toy banana. "This one, please!" Joshua put it in her basket. "Thank you for waiting at my shop," he said.

Then Mia gave him the banana back. "Now you are the shopper," she said.

Joshua laughed. Two people, two jobs, and they could swap! Joshua put the banana in his basket and walked to the play kitchen. "One soup, please," he said, and knocked on the little toy door.

story:

Charlotte pressed the button. The screen lit up. She heard a soft sound. "I did it!" she said. Milo's mom showed her the little drawing app. Charlotte tapped it. A white page opened. She drew a green hill with her finger. Then she drew a yellow sun over the hill.

The tablet blinked. The screen went dark. "It's tired," said Milo. "It needs the charger." Charlotte found the charger cord on the shelf. She carried it to Milo's mom. The mom plugged the charger into the wall. Charlotte put the tablet down on the table. "All done," she said. "I can draw the last cloud tomorrow."

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Sarah ran into the library. She wanted a book about dogs. Dogs were her favorite animals.

At the picture table, two kids were arguing. A boy held a card with an apple on it. "It goes with the fruits," he said. "No, it goes with the foods," said a girl. They each pulled a little. The card began to bend.

Sarah looked at the table. There was a picture of bread by the foods. There was a picture of grapes by the fruits. Then she saw something. There was a rough basket with two labels on it. One label said foods. The other said fruits.

"Put it here," Sarah said. She pointed at the basket. The boy set the apple inside. The apple sat in both groups at once.

"It fits," said the girl. "It fits two ways," said the boy. They clapped. Sarah clapped too.

Then Sarah found her dog book. She hugged it tight. "Home time," she said.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Max sat at Grandma's kitchen table. He had a big yellow pencil. He wanted to write his name, just like his big brother could.

"Can I write M?" he asked.

Grandma drew a big M. But it had small dots inside it. "Try this," she said.

Max held the pencil. Grandma moved his fingers. "Thumb here," she said. "Now go over the dots."

Max drew his pencil on the dots. The dots turned into a line. The line turned into an M! Max looked at it. Did his hand do that?

"Again," said Max.

He traced the dotted A. It worked too. He traced the X. Now his whole name sat on the paper.

"My name!" said Max. He held it up. "Dry it?" he asked.

"It will dry fast," said Grandma.

Max waved the paper in the air. His brother came in and looked.

"Did you make that?" his brother asked.

Max grinned and pointed at the M. "Me," he said. "All by me."

Grandpa said, "Try telling Mia what to play."

story:

Then she saw a tall white hat on the shelf. She put it on her head. "I am the cook!" she said. Ben gave her a wooden spoon. Mia gave her the doll. "The baby is hungry," said Mia. Willow stirred a pretend pot. "Soup is ready!" she said. The doll got a bottle and went to sleep.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Gianna was at Mia's birthday party. On the rug sat a big box of blocks. A boy named Leo grabbed the box first. Gianna wanted the blocks too. She reached out her hand to grab them.

Then she stopped. She thought hard. "Can we both play?" she asked. Leo looked at the box. "But there is only one box," he said. "Can one box be for two kids?" Gianna asked herself. She looked at the rug. It looked big and empty. "Let's make one big tower," she said. "Together?"

Leo nodded. "Together," he said. They sat side by side. Gianna put one block down. Leo put the next block on top. "One for you, one for me," said Gianna. "One for you, one for me," said Leo.

The tower grew tall. It got so tall it looked thin at the top. Then it wobbled. "Oops," said Leo. The blocks fell down with a clatter. The two friends laughed. "Let's dig in the box and start again," said Gianna. They built the tower up, up, up. Then they clapped. "We made it together," said Leo. "Best tower ever," said Gianna.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Olivia went to the garden center with her dad. The sun felt warm on her face. There were pots and seeds and little plants everywhere. Olivia picked a packet of carrot seeds. "I want a carrot garden," she said. Dad smiled and got a big bag of soft brown soil.

At home, they filled a long box with soil. Olivia poked little holes with her finger. She dropped one seed in each hole. Then she covered them up, pat, pat, pat. The soil smelled like rain. Dad said, "All done!" But Olivia forgot one thing.

Every morning Olivia ran to the box. She looked and looked. Nothing grew. The soil was dry and crumbly. "Where are my carrots?" she asked. Her tummy felt worried. Then she saw the sky. The weather was hot. The sun could burn her shoulders, dad said, so he put a hat on her head.

Dad handed her a small green watering can. It went "swish, swish," a soft, loud splash on the soil. Olivia watered the seeds every day. The soil turned dark and damp.

One morning, tiny green leaves popped up. Two leaves, then five, then ten! Olivia jumped up and down. "They grew!" she called. Dad gave her a thumbs up. Olivia patted the soil gently. "More water tomorrow," she said, and carried her little can inside.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Ivy sat on the grass by Grandpa Joe's stone. The stone was warm and dry in the sun. Mom set out bread, apples, and cheese.

"Now we hold hands," said Mom. "We say the blessing, like Grandpa Joe did."

Ivy held Mom's hand. She held Dad's hand. But her mouth stayed shut. The blessing felt too big for her. Dad said the words. Mom said the words. Ivy only listened.

She looked at the bread. She thought and thought. Who made this bread? A baker made it. Who grew the apples? A farmer grew them. The sun helped too.

Dad handed her the bread. "Your turn, Ivy. You can choose your own words."

Ivy took a big breath. "Thank you for the bread," she said. "One, thank you for the apples. Two, thank you for the cheese. Three, thank you for the sun."

Mom squeezed her hand. Dad smiled a big smile. Then Mom said, "One, thank you for Grandpa Joe." Dad said, "Two, thank you for Ivy's words."

Ivy felt the squeeze go around. Mom squeezed her hand. She squeezed Dad's hand. Dad squeezed back. The thank-you went around and around, like a circle.

Ivy bit her apple. It was sweet and cold. The wind moved the grass by the stone.

"Again tomorrow?" she asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Every day."

Ivy waved at the stone. "Bye, Grandpa Joe. Thank you for the blessing."

story:
Maverick ran to Grandma's toy box. He found a soft gray pig with a floppy ear. "Mine!" said his cousin Nia. "No, mine!" said Maverick. Grandma sat down between them. "Play pretend with it," she said. Nia held the pig first. She wrapped it in a small blanket. "The pig is sick," Nia said. Maverick felt the pig's ear. It was warm and fuzzy. He patted it softly. "The pig is sleeping," he said. "No, the pig is hungry," said Nia. Maverick made a sad face. Then he had an idea. "The pig is hungry, then sleepy," he said. Nia smiled and clapped her hands. "Yes! Then it swings on the swing!"

Nia found a tiny cup. Maverick fed the pig pretend oats. He made a little yum yum sound. Then the pig got very sleepy. Nia rocked it in her arms. "Shh," she whispered. Grandma hummed a quiet song. Maverick covered the pig with his own jacket. The pig's ear felt soft against his hand. "Goodnight, pig," said Maverick. "Goodnight," said Nia, in her most polite voice. Grandma gave them both warm hugs. "You two agreed on the game," she said. "That was kind sharing." Maverick snuggled close to Grandma. Outside, a bird sang at the window. The pig slept and slept. "Nice pig," whispered Maverick.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Emma stood by the camp table. She wanted to make pancakes for her family. Daddy was there to help. Daddy lit the little camp stove. Emma stayed back from the hot pan.

First came the flour. Emma tipped the bag. Too much flour puffed out. The bowl looked like a snow cloud. "Oh no," said Emma. "It went too fast."

Daddy handed her a big cup. "Fill this," he said. Emma scooped flour into the cup. She made it level with her finger. The cup held just the right amount. Then she used a little spoon for the sugar. One spoon, not a river of sugar. Daddy cracked the eggs. Emma poured the milk from her cup, slow and steady.

The batter went drip, drip into the pan. Daddy flipped each pancake. A green frog hopped by and watched too. Soon the pancakes were warm and golden. Emma took a taste. "Yum!" she said. "The cup helped me make them just right." Daddy gave her a big hug.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Anna was playing outside on a windy day. Dust blew all around. Anna rubbed her face with her hands. Something small got in her eye. "Ouch," said Anna. It felt scratchy and sad.

Mama helped Anna blink and blink. Then the dust was gone. Anna looked in the little mirror. She saw tiny hairs on her eyelids. "What are these?" she asked. "They are my eyelashes," she said.

Anna blinked again. Her eyelashes went down, then up. They touched her cheek, soft as a feather. Did they stop the dust? Anna ran her fingers over them. She could feel them tickle.

Inside, Anna smelled warm cookies. She heard the timer ring. Mama gave her one cookie. Anna took a little bite. It tasted sweet. Anna smiled. She did not want to lose her cookie, so she ate it all up, blinking her happy lashes.

"Hello, little lashes," said Anna.

story:
Jake was in the playroom with his friend Mia. They wanted to play house. Jake got the small blue pot. Mia got the gray blanket for the bed.

"I want to be the parent," said Jake. "I want to be the parent too," said Mia. They both held the pot. Neither one would let go. The pot went clunk on the floor.

Then Jake had an idea. "You can be the parent first," he said. "I will be the baby. Then we can switch." Mia smiled. She wrapped Jake in the gray blanket. He pretended to sleep. Then she fed him pretend soup from a little cup.

Next it was Jake's turn to be the parent. Mia curled up with her robot toy. She made the robot cry like a baby. Jake patted the robot softly. "There, there," he said. "Time for a nap." He covered them both with the blanket. Mia closed her eyes and snored a big pretend snore. Jake giggled and turned off the pretend light with a click.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Austin ran to the playground. It was a big playground. Austin was small, but he could run fast. "Look at me go!" he said.

Dad sat on the bench with a big water bottle. "The sun is hot today," said Dad. Austin touched the slide. The slide was hot too. So he went to the little slide in the shade. That slide was cool. Down he went, slow and easy.

Then Austin saw a puddle. He jumped in it. Splash! His shoes were wet. His socks were wet. "My socks are all wet," said Austin. Dad opened his bag. "Here are dry socks," said Dad. Austin sat on the bench. Off came the wet socks. On went the dry socks. Dry socks felt warm and cozy. "Dry socks are better," said Austin. Dad laughed. "Let's go find the horsey," he said. Austin rode the bouncy horse up and down. He did not want to ride alone, so Dad held his hand. Then they walked home, slow and happy, all dry.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Nova went to her friend Mia's house. Mia had a big cardboard box. "It's a car!" said Mia. She turned a paper plate. Vroom, vroom!

Nova shook her head. "It's a house," she said. She put her teddy bear inside. "Teddy lives here now."

"But I want a car," said Mia. "But I want a house," said Nova. They both frowned. The box just sat there.

Then Mia had an idea. "You go first," she said. "Then me." Nova smiled. She patted teddy and gave him a bottle. She crawled in and rocked him to sleep.

Then Nova climbed out. "Now it's your turn," she said. Mia jumped in. "Beep, beep! The bus is here!" said Mia. Nova ran around and waved. "Stop the bus! I want to ride!"

The box stopped. Nova climbed in too. Now the bus had two riders. They drove all the way to the kitchen for a snack.

Later, Mia's mom came in early to check on them. "Where did you two go?" she asked. Mia pointed at the box. "To the moon," said Nova. "And back," said Mia. "Room for one more," said Nova, and she held up teddy.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Liam ran into daycare. Today a firefighter was coming to visit! He felt so excited. He jumped up and down. He bounced on his toes. He shouted, "The firefighter is coming!"

Teacher Mia said, "Liam, you are so excited. But bouncing makes you extra noisy. Let's find a calm way to wait."

She put a big box of blocks on the table. "You can pat the table softly while we wait," she said.

Liam patted the table. Pat, pat, pat. It felt smooth and cool. He took a big breath. Then he patted again.

"The firefighter is coming," he said, nice and quiet this time.

Then the door opened. A firefighter in a big shiny hat walked in. Liam felt excited again. His feet wanted to jump! But he patted his knees instead. Pat, pat, pat.

"Hello, friends," said the firefighter.

Liam waved. "I waited so good," he whispered to Teacher Mia.

She smiled and gave him a hug. "You did, Liam."

The firefighter showed everyone her red truck through the window. It was big and loud and bright.

"Truck!" said Liam. He clapped his hands.

"Would you like to try on my hat?" the firefighter asked.

She set the big hat on Liam's head. It was heavy and warm. Liam grinned a big grin.

"I'm a firefighter!" he said.

At nap time, Liam curled up on his mat. He patted his teddy bear softly. Pat, pat, pat.

"The truck goes beep, beep," he said. His eyes closed.

Teacher Mia tucked his blanket in. "Sleep tight, big helper," she said.

story:
Emile sat at the big art table. He wanted to draw a sun. A sun needs a big round circle.

Emile picked up his crayon. He drew a circle. It came out wobbly. It looked like a squished egg. He tried again. Wobbly again. Emile frowned at his paper.

Then he saw Mia's cup on the table. It was a round cup. Emile held his paper next to it. He put his crayon at the bottom of the cup. He traced all the way around the bottom of the cup. He lifted the cup up. There it was. A big round circle! A real one!

Emile drew triangle rays around his circle. Yellow triangle rays, just like the sun. Mia drew a square window beside his sun. Tom drew a rectangle door. The teacher tapped the picture with her phone to show Emile's mom later. "Look at my sun!" Emile said. He held the cup up high.

story:
Eva ran to the swings with Grandma. The swings were near a tall forest of trees. One, two, three, she pumped her legs. The swing went high. "Look at me!" she said.

Next Eva wanted the slide. The sun sat on the slide. Grandma put her hand on it. "Too hot," said Grandma. They waited in the shade. They waited and waited. Eva counted clouds. One, two, three. At last the slide felt cool. Down Eva went. Fast!

Then Eva saw something on the picnic table. Little red dots, like candy. "Grandma, come look," she said. She did not touch them. Grandma looked. She put them in her pocket. "Good girl. Only a grown-up gives you medicine."

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Zoe sat at the paint table. She wanted to paint a magic sun. She had red, yellow, and blue paint.

"Red, yellow, blue," she said softly, like a song. She touched each cup as she named it. Then she dipped her brush in the yellow.

Zoe put a big yellow circle on her paper. It looked like the sun. Now she wanted orange. She had heard that red and yellow could make orange, like magic.

She dipped her brush in the red. She painted beside the yellow. But the red came out brown and muddy. Her sun looked dirty. Zoe frowned at it.

She looked at her brush. It was still yellow at the tip. She rinsed it in the water cup. The water turned cloudy yellow. The brush came out clean.

She dipped the clean brush in red. She painted a red stripe on the yellow sun. The red touched the yellow and made orange. Real orange, bright like a leaf in autumn.

"Magic!" whispered Zoe.

Tommy at the next seat was frowning. His yellow had turned muddy too. Zoe leaned over. "Wash your brush first," she said, polite and quiet. Tommy rinsed his brush. His yellow came out bright and clean.

Zoe painted a green frog with her rinsed brush. "Look," she said. "My sun is orange and my frog says hello."

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Sebastian stood in the backyard with a red beanbag. He wanted to toss it into the hoop on the grass. He threw it. The beanbag fell outside the circle. "Oh no," said Sebastian. He sat down on the step.

Then he got up. He picked up the beanbag. He threw it again. It missed again. He threw it one more time. It missed one more time. But his throw went closer to the hoop.

Sebastian was busy trying. Throw, pick up, throw again. Each time, the beanbag went a little closer. Then one throw went up and dropped right into the hoop. "I did it!" said Sebastian. He jumped with both feet.

Next Dad rolled him a big blue ball. Sebastian tried to catch it with both hands. It bumped his arms and fell. He tried again. It fell again. Then he held his hands out wide. The ball came right into them. Sebastian hugged the ball tight. "Again, Dad!" he said.

story:
Ivy ran to the swings. It was summer and the sun was warm. "One swing, two swings, three swings," she said. She wanted Saturday to come. On Saturday, Dad would bring her best friend Mia to the playground.

"Is Saturday tomorrow?" she asked Mom. Mom smiled and shook her head. "Count the days with me," Mom said. Ivy held up her little hand. Mom touched each finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven days in a week. Ivy wiggled all seven fingers.

Then Ivy saw a boy drop his juice cup. It began to spill on the sand. "Careful!" said his mama, wiping it up. Ivy ran to get the boy a paper cup from the water fountain. "Thank you," the boy said. He gave her a big smile. Then he helped count petals on a flower. "Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ivy laughed. She looked at her fingers again. Seven more sleeps until Saturday. She swung high in the sky. "One, two, three!" she called to the clouds.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Olivier dug a little hole. He dropped a seed in. Then he patted the soil on top. "Grow, little seed," he said.

Olivier came back the next day. Nothing was there. He came back after many days. A tiny green leaf peeked out! "Mama, look!" he said. He watered it with his small can.

A weed grew next to his plant. It had a pink flower on top. "I will pull you out," said Olivier. He pulled it, gently. Up it came. Long stringy roots hung from the bottom! "Wow," said Olivier. "What are these?" He touched them. They were soft and wet. His plant had roots down in the soil too, he thought. So that is how it held on.

Olivier patted the soil again. He ate a cookie by his little green leaf. "Stay in the ground, roots," he said. "Grow down deep."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Eliana wanted the big book on Grandma's shelf. It had a purple cover. Grandma took it down and opened it.

"Read it, Grandma!" said Eliana.

Grandma read the first page. "The little bear crawled under the blanket." Then she turned the page. Eliana saw the little black marks. The marks sat on the page like tiny ants.

Later, Grandpa sat down. "My turn," he said. He opened the book from the front. He read page one. "The little bear crawled under the blanket."

Eliana's eyes went wide. "Same words!"

"Same words," said Grandpa.

Eliana looked at the page. A map was on the next page. The bear was looking for his honey.

"I read it," said Eliana. She pointed at the ants. "Little bear crawls under!"

Grandma clapped. "You read it, Eliana!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Isaac sat in the waiting room with his father. He held his favorite teddy bear tight. Today he would get a shot, and that made him worry.

Then the doctor came in. A funny tube hung around her neck. "What is that?" Isaac asked. The doctor smiled. "It is for listening." She put the little ends in her ears. She held the other end on Isaac's chest.

Thump, thump. Thump, thump. Isaac heard his own heart beating inside him. "I hear it!" he said. He listened to his teddy bear too, but the bear was quiet.

Then it was time for the shot. Isaac sat on his father's lap and hugged his bear. The doctor said, "One, two, three." It was done, quick as that. She put a small bandage on his arm.

"You were so brave," his father said. Isaac looked at the tube around the doctor's neck. "Can I hear my heart one more time?" he asked.

The doctor put the ends in his ears again. Thump, thump. Thump, thump. "Still going," said Isaac.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Elena woke up and saw white. Snow! Lots and lots of snow. "No school today!" said Mama. "It is a snow day!" Elena jumped out of bed. She put on her boots and her red coat. She ran outside fast, fast, fast. Then her boot slid. Whoosh! Elena fell down on the icy sidewalk. "Ouch," she said. She felt a little grumpy. Why did she fall? The ice was slippery. That was why.

Elena stood up slowly. She tried small steps. Slip, no. Slow steps. Careful steps. "Slow like a turtle," she said. It worked! She did not fall. Next came her friend Sam. Sam ran. Sam slipped too. "Walk slow!" Elena called. "Slow like a turtle!" Sam took small, slow steps. Sam did not fall. "Yay!" they both shouted.

They found a big stick. Elena let Sam hold the stick. They tapped the snow. Tap, tap, tap. The snow popped off the bushes. "Do it again!" said Sam. Tap, tap, tap. Then Mama called from the door, "Hot cocoa time!" Elena and Sam walked home, slow like a turtle, all the way to the warm house.

activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Matteo put on his red shoes. One shoe went on his left foot. One shoe went on his right foot. Today was his first day of school. His tummy felt funny. He hid behind Mama's leg.

"Ready?" Mama asked. Matteo shook his head. A lady in a yellow sweater opened the big door. "Hello," she said. "I am Miss Jo." Matteo peeked out. He did not know her name before. Now he knew it. Miss Jo. Miss Jo held out her hand. Matteo put his small hand in it.

They walked to the toy corner. Miss Jo got him a truck. Then she got him a block. Matteo pushed the truck on the dark green rug. It rolled far. He pushed it again. It rolled again. Then Matteo turned to Miss Jo. "Hello," he said. "Hello, Matteo," said Miss Jo. He smiled and pushed the truck one more time.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Jasper lost his special red car. He looked on the swing. He looked by the sand. "One, two, three, look," said Jasper. No car.

Miss Jo came to help. "Where did it go?" she asked. Jasper shrugged his little shoulders. Then he saw the playhouse. It had a little green couch inside. Jasper gasped. The couch was low. Small toys could roll right under it.

"One, two, three, look," said Jasper. He got down on his knees. He peeked under the couch. There it was! The red car sat in the dark, by a small brown leaf. "Miss Jo! My car rolled under here!"

Jasper reached in and pulled the car out. He held it tight. Miss Jo smiled. Then Jasper pushed the car down the little slide. "Whee!" said Jasper. "Go, car, go!"

story:
William wanted a turn on the red trike. Three friends were in line by the door. William ran fast to the front. "No, William," said Mia. "I am first. You are last." William looked at the line. Mia was in front. Then Ben. Then Sam. Then William.

William walked back to his spot. He put his hands in his pockets. He waited. Mia rode the trike around the rug. She pedaled past the blocks. Then she got off. "Your turn, Ben," said Mia. Ben rode the trike. He rang the little bell. Then Ben got off too.

Sam had a turn. Then Sam got off. Now it was William's turn. William sat on the red trike. He gripped the handles. He pedaled past the shelf and past the toy barn. The bell went clink, clink. Mia clapped her hands. "Nice riding, William," she said. William rode one big loop, then stopped. "Your turn again, Mia," he said. He stood at the back of the line and waited.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Florence stood in the backyard with her dad. "Let's play the senses game," said Dad. "One, eyes to see. Two, ears to hear. Three, nose to smell. Four, tongue to taste. Five, hands to touch." Florence clapped. "I can guess them all!"

"I see the sky," said Florence. "I use my eyes." Then she wanted to see the sun up close. She looked up. The sun was too bright. Her eyes blinked and blinked. Dad held up his hand like a hat over her eyes. "Never look straight at the sun," he said. "It can hurt your eyes." Florence looked at Dad's pink sneaker instead. "I see your pink shoe," she said. "My eyes are safe."

Next came ears. Florence heard a bee buzz. "Buzz, buzz, my ears hear it!" Then her nose smelled the flowers. Then her hands touched the warm grass. "I can touch the grass, but not the sun," said Florence. Dad laughed. "That's right, clever girl." Florence patted the grass again. "Five senses, all done. That was fun!"

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Connor ran to the swings at the playground. The big swing was taken. A girl was on it, going high. Connor stopped and watched. "Can I have a turn?" he asked. "You can come next," the girl said. "I will count to ten, then stop."

Connor waited. He counted with her. One, two, three. The swing went slow. Four, five, six. The swing went lower. Ten! The girl jumped off. "Your turn now," she said. Connor got on the swing. It was hard to start at first. He pumped his legs again and again. Then he went up, up, up.

A small boy came to the swings too. He had no turn. He stood and watched Connor. Connor saw him there. So Connor counted to ten, just like the girl. Then he stopped the swing. "Your turn now," he said.

The small boy got on. Connor gave him a push. "Is this a present for me?" the boy asked. "No," said Connor. "It is just my turn, given to you." The boy laughed and swung high.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Sophie put on her red team shirt. Her grandpa tied her shoes. The sky was big and gray. The park had green grass.

The game began. Sophie ran to the ball. She kicked it hard. The ball rolled and rolled. It went toward the big net. Sophie clapped and cheered.

Then the coach waved her hands. "Sophie, that net is not ours," she said. Sophie looked around. "Which net is mine?" she asked. Her friend Ben pointed to the other side. "Kick the ball that way," he said.

Sophie picked up the ball. She set it down again. She turned her whole body. Then she kicked the ball to the far net. The ball went in. The team all shouted for joy. Ben did not cry. He laughed and hugged Sophie.

Sophie waved to her grandpa. He waved back from the bench. "Again, again!" Sophie said. She ran to get the ball.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Olivier was at the doctor's office. He was not late. He sat on a big chair with his mom.

Olivier saw fish in a tank. He used his eyes to see the blue fish swim. He heard a loud noise. It was the doctor's paper cutter. It went "Whirr!" Olivier did not like the loud sound.

He put his hands over his ears. "Hmm," he thought. The sound got quiet. He took his hands off. The whirr was loud again. He put his hands back on. Quiet again! Olivier smiled.

The doctor came in. "Hello, Olivier," she said. "Open your mouth so I can see inside." Olivier opened his mouth. "Say ahh," said the doctor. "Ahh," said Olivier. She looked with a little light.

Then the doctor gave him a sticker. It was a plane. Olivier touched it. It felt smooth. He sniffed it. It smelled like nothing much. "Can I keep it?" he asked. "Yes," said the doctor.

Olivier drew a picture while mom talked. He drew the fish, the plane, and his two hands on his ears. "That is me," he said. He held the picture up so his mom could see it with her eyes.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Zayn stood on the big ferry with his mama and baba. The boat went chug, chug across the water. Zayn held his small blue bag. Inside were his socks, his cap, and a snack.

"Where is my red car?" Zayn asked. He looked in the bag. No car. His tummy felt wobbly, like jelly. He wanted his car for the trip.

Baba knelt down beside him. "Let's look together," Baba said. They searched the bag, sock by sock. Then Zayn felt something hard in his shoe. He pulled off his shoe and shook it. Out fell the red car, and one little seed from the park.

"My car!" Zayn said. He laughed and hugged it. The seed had come from a stinky fruit tree they sat under yesterday. Now it sat in his hand, small and round.

When the ferry reached the other side, the family walked to their little room. Then they got home after the trip, and it was time to unpack. Zayn put his socks in the drawer. He put his cap on the hook. He put his red car on the shelf, right next to the seed.

Mama helped him stir the pot for dinner, safe and slow. Zayn put the seed into a cup of dirt by the window. "Grow, little seed," he whispered.

story:
Hannah stood in the big school gym. A small beanbag sat in her hand. She wanted to throw it into the hoop on the floor. She threw it. It flew past the hoop. "Oh no," said Hannah. "Can I try again?" she asked. "Yes," said Teacher Jo. "Try again."

Hannah threw the beanbag. This time it landed in the hoop. "I did it!" she said. Teacher Jo clapped.

Then Teacher Jo rolled a big ball to Hannah. Hannah's hands were in her pockets. The ball rolled right past her. Hannah pulled her hands out. She held her arms out wide. Her hands were open. activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Asher went to the library with his dad. Today was craft day. Asher wanted to make a butterfly. The librarian gave him paper and paint.

Asher painted one wing. It was red and blue, like a little rainbow. Then his tummy felt hungry. "Snack first," said Dad. Asher set his paper down. It closed in half while he ate his crackers.

When Asher came back, he opened the paper. He scratched his head. There were two wings now! Both sides looked the same. The wet paint had copied itself.

Asher tried it again. He painted one wing green. He folded the paper. He pressed it with his hands. He opened it. Two green wings, both the same!

"I made a butterfly," said Asher. He showed it to the librarian. "Two wings, just alike," she said. A little girl next to him had no paint left. Asher shared his green. "Fold it," he told her. She folded her paper and opened it. "Two wings!" she said. Asher held his butterfly up high.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
William sat in his car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump. "Look at the bag, William," said Mom. William looked in the toy bag next to him.

He saw cars. One car, two cars, three cars. They were all small and round. Then he saw something long and yellow. It was not a car. It was a banana! "Mom, a banana is in with my cars!" Mom laughed softly. "That is the odd one out," she said. "It does not belong."

William held the banana up. "You do not belong with the cars," he said. "You belong with the food." Mom said they would put it in the lunch bag at the next stop.

The car went on and on. William played a game. He looked at his snack box. He saw grapes, crackers, and one little toy duck. "Duck, you are the odd one out! You are a toy, not a snack." The duck fell onto the floor. "Quack," said William, in a small duck voice.

At the stop, Mom put the banana in the lunch bag. "Good job, William." William patted the banana. "Bye bye, odd one out." Then he hugged his toy duck tight. The car door closed with a soft click, and off they went again.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Evelyn went to the park with Dad. She carried her blue bunny under one arm. Bunny had one ear that flopped down.

Evelyn ran to the slide. She climbed up. She slid down. Then she looked for bunny. Bunny was gone.

Evelyn wanted to run and look all alone. She stopped. She ran to Dad instead. "Bunny is lost!" she said. "Help me look."

Dad took her hand. They looked at the slide first. One slide, no bunny. They looked at the swings next. Two swings, no bunny. They looked at the big rock. One rock, and there sat bunny!

A boy had set bunny on the rock. "I found it on the grass," he said. "I put it here so someone would see it."

Evelyn hugged her blue bunny tight. "Thank you," she said. Dad smiled. "Good job telling me first," he said.

Evelyn slid down the slide one more time. She held bunny up high. "Wheee!" said Evelyn.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Noah ran onto the green field. Coach Mia was there with a big smile. All the kids sat in a line.

Coach Mia put one red ball on the grass. Noah wanted it first. He ran fast and grabbed it. He held it tight with both hands.

Sam started to cry. "My turn," Sam said. Noah felt mad inside. He wanted the ball so much. Coach Mia knelt down next to them. "Sam can play with the ball too," she said softly. She held up her clipboard. "I will write your names on my list. Then we know whose turn is next."

Noah looked at the ball. He looked at Sam. Sam had no ball at all. Noah took a big breath. He rolled the ball to Sam. Sam stopped crying. Sam kicked the ball back. Then Noah kicked it again.

"Nice pass, Noah," said Coach Mia. Noah laughed. Sam laughed too. The ball went back and forth like a little boat on the ocean.

At the end, Coach Mia gave them both a drink of water. "Same time next week," she said. Noah waved to Sam. "See you, Sam," he said. Then he held his dad's hand all the way home.
